title: Pauri 29, meaning: wisdom for food
hook: let wisdom be your food and compassion the one who serves it; the music sounds in every heart (Japji 29)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 29, naad. Your line was bhugat giaan, wisdom is the meal. Did you say it before a bite, and did you notice who served you? Today, what the whole stanza means. Day two hundred twelve.

A school cook slips an extra scoop onto a tray because the kid in front of her looks like they've had a rough morning. A grandmother won't sit down until every plate is full. An uncle at a wedding keeps coming back with the tray. Years later, it can be the hands that stay in memory, more than the food. The same rice tastes different when it's handed over by someone who wants you fed. In a gurdwara's langar, people sit in rows, and volunteers come down the line with a bucket and a ladle. Pauri 29 puts a server like that at the center of its meal.
screen: `THE EXTRA SCOOP.` → `THE HANDS STAY IN MEMORY.` → `THE LADLE IN LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak is speaking to yogis, in their own camp words. Their shared meal was bhugat, so he says: let wisdom be your bhugat. Not a rule, not a diet. The thing that actually feeds you is understanding. Then he names the server: daiaa bhanddaaran, compassion is the keeper of the stores. Put the two together. Wisdom without compassion is a locked pantry. Someone knows a great deal and hands none of it out, or hands it out with a sneer. In Pauri 29, wisdom is only a meal when compassion holds the ladle. Then the horn. The yogis blew a horn to sound the naad, the note they listened for in meditation. Nanak says: ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad. It's already sounding, in every heart. No horn needed. The next line keeps the food picture going. The yogis honored their great teachers as Naths, masters. Nanak says the One is the true Nath, holding every creature on His string. And the miraculous powers some yogis worked for, riddhi and siddhi? Nanak calls them avaraa saad, other flavors. Tasty, maybe, but not the meal. Then a wide line: sanjog vijog, meeting and parting, both keep the world turning, and each of us receives our share as it is written. And the refrain again, the yogis' own greeting turned toward God: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him. So the menu is short. Wisdom to eat, compassion to serve it, and a note already playing in you.
screen: `WISDOM IS THE MEAL.` · `COMPASSION HOLDS THE LADLE.` · `THE NOTE IS ALREADY PLAYING.` · `POWERS ARE JUST OTHER FLAVORS.` · then, large: `COMPASSION SERVES THE FOOD.`

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one small bite or one sip, and take it slowly. If not, picture your next meal. As you taste it, think of one thing you understand now that you didn't a year ago, and who handed it to you: a teacher, a parent, a friend, a stranger. Let the taste and the thanks sit together. Then rest, breathing, and listen for the note Nanak says is already sounding. The bell holds the time.
Nath, master, the yogis' name for their teacher. Wisdom as the meal, compassion as the one who serves it, a note in every heart, and miraculous powers called nothing more than other flavors.
Your line: compassion serves the food. Today, when you know something someone else needs, hand it over kindly, the way you'd want to be served. Day two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; in the gurdwara's langar, people still sit in rows and are served by volunteers with a ladle, which many hear as a living picture of compassion serving the meal.

myth: Pauri 29 praises miraculous powers as the goal
Nanak calls them avaraa saad: other flavors, not the meal.
in Pauri 29, the note sounds in every heart
ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad: no horn needed.
Nanak calls the One the true Nath, the true master
he borrows the yogis' own word for their great teachers.

fork.setup: the yogis prize ridh sidh, miraculous powers. what does Nanak call them in Pauri 29?
options: other flavors, not the real meal.
fork.reveal: avaraa saad: other tastes. the stanza keeps its food picture: wisdom is the meal, powers are a side dish that distracts.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 29: in every heart the note is sounding.

trapdoor: what you thought: eat smart food.
what it means: wisdom is what feeds you, and compassion is what hands it out.
what a scholar hears: every image answers a yogi practice: the camp meal, the horn's naad, the Nath masters, and the prized powers dismissed as avaraa saad.

notes: English of the stanza is paraphrase; Gurmukhi words quoted in transliteration. Macauliffe 1909 not quoted because not verified word for word.
'aap naath naathee sabh jaa kee' paraphrased as the One being the true Nath holding every creature on His string; the string reading of naathee follows common commentary. Confirm.
ridh sidh avaraa saad glossed as powers being 'other flavors'; confirm the Keeper's preferred gloss.
Naad glossed as the note Nath yogis sounded on the horn and listened for in meditation; confirm.
